newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels say peaceful solution chances are 50-50.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say peaceful solution chances are 50-50.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's house in Lima said on Tuesday that a military assault on the residence could be imminent but they still saw plenty of room for a negotiated solution.

"Right now there is a real danger of intervention" by armed forces in a bid to free the captives, said Isaac Velazco, the international spokesman for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas who have been holed up in the mansion with the hostages since Dec. 17.

But he also said that he thought recent tough talk by President Alberto Fujimori, who stressed he would not cave in to the captors' demands, was mere posturing that would be normal in any negotiating process.
"Chances that the government opts for a military intervention or for negotiations are 50-50," Velazco said, speaking to Reuters in a telephone interview from Germany.
He said the rebels had "ways of knowing" that an attack remained part of the government's options, but would not discuss details.

Although nearly four months have gone by without any apparent major progress, he said headway was being made and the two sides remained inclined to compromise on the main sticking point -- the release from jail of 450 MRTA rebels.
"Important advances have been made," said Velazco, citing the ongoing talks with negotiators and what he perceived as a government willingness to free MRTA rebels despite Fujimori's statements.
"We take five steps forward, then 10 steps back, then three steps forward again," said Velazco. "It takes a lot of patience."
The two sides have not held face-to-face talks now for nearly a month and blame each other for the failure.
Velazco's remarks contrasted with those of a government official, who reiterated Fujimori's public stance that not a single MRTA rebel would be freed from prison.
"We will not cave in, we will not free the MRTA inmates," said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

However, he admitted that Fujimori was under pressure from Tokyo to make concessions in order to put an end to the crisis. Ambassador Morihisa Aoki is one of the two dozen Japanese nationals being held by the MRTA at his residence.

Velazco said media reports that the 20-odd fighters under the command of MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa inside the mansion were training to get ready for a military assault were possibly true, but he denied that any new MRTA commandos had been ferried to Lima to back them up.

"No new units were moved recently," he said, adding that MRTA fighters have been positioned in strategic sites since early in the crisis and that it would be foolish for them to deploy commandos now that the armed forces were fully alert.
The army's intelligence service, where the media reports allegedly originated, declined to comment.

If a military assault on the residence did materialise, the rebels would resist down to the last combatant and try to preserve the lives of the hostages, Velasco said. "Although it should be noted that in an attack in the middle of the night it is very difficult to say who is who."

The government official said some of the younger rebels' morale was declining, but Velazco said it was high. "Even if they have to stay put for ... a year or two, rest assured their morale will not give in," he said.
Cerpa said on Monday there was no chance of resuming direct talks until the government showed the "political will" to address their demand for the release of MRTA inmates.
Fujimori said on Sunday that he would not send his crisis negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, for talks until he was confident that negotiations were moving forward.
